prompt:
You review acceptance criteria for an HTTP API against its source code, and surface what a tester needs to know before writing tests.

Inputs:
- The requirements (story) and the criteria extracted from them, without code knowledge.
- A route index (method, path, handler, file:line).
- The full in-scope source with line numbers.

Produce four things.

1. criterion_routes: for each criterion id, the routes ("METHOD /path" exactly as in the index) it exercises.

2. findings: things a tester must know, each with code evidence (file and line from the numbered source). Kinds:
   - missing_error_path: an input or state the requirements don't cover that the code handles, or fails to handle.
   - rule_interaction: two rules that combine in a way the requirements don't settle.
   - story_code_conflict: the code does something different from what a criterion says.
   - suspected_defect: behaviour that looks wrong whatever the requirements say (e.g. an unhandled input that would produce a server error, a missing authorization check, a limit with no bound).
   - no_requirement: a behaviour or route the requirements never mention.

3. observed: criteria derived from the code, for behaviour the requirements don't cover but a tester should pin down. Only add observed criteria for important behaviour the story leaves out. Describe what the code does; never present a suspected defect as expected behaviour: set suspected_defect true and give alternatives (what should plausibly happen instead). Every observed criterion needs evidence. Every suspected_defect finding about behaviour the requirements cover must also appear here as an observed criterion with suspected_defect true.

4. questions: decisions a human must make because the requirements are ambiguous. Ask only when there are at least two plausible answers AND the answer changes an expected value or whether a test passes. For each: the criterion id it is about ("" if none), a short `about` key, why it matters, the plausible options, and what the answer changes (expected_value or pass_fail).

Rules for test design to apply while reviewing:
- Every input with a size, length or count: check the minimum, the maximum, and just outside both.
- Every route: check each kind of caller (anonymous, ordinary user, the resource's owner, superuser).
- Every write: check what happens on conflict with existing data (duplicates, uniqueness).
- Every list: check ordering, empty results, and how many items one request can return.
- Every token or session: check expiry and what happens after it.
- A server error (5xx) in response to client input is never expected behaviour.


Criteria that AmbiguityLint flagged (consider asking about them): {"C-1": ["missing_error_path"], "C-2": ["missing_actor"], "C-3": ["missing_actor"], "C-4": ["missing_error_path"], "C-6": ["missing_error_path"], "C-7": ["missing_error_path"], "C-8": ["no_observable_outcome"], "C-9": ["no_observable_outcome", "missing_actor", "missing_error_path"], "C-10": ["missing_actor"], "C-11": ["missing_actor", "unspecified_boundary"], "C-12": ["vague_quantifier", "missing_error_path"], "C-13": ["vague_quantifier", "missing_error_path"], "C-14": ["vague_quantifier", "missing_error_path"], "C-15": ["vague_quantifier"]}

# Items and accounts — user story

> Draft for review. Written from the product's README and dashboard description only,
> not from its code. Status: awaiting the product owner's approval.

## Logging in

As a registered user, I want to log in with my email and password so that I can manage my items.

- A user who gives the right email and password receives an access token.
- A wrong password, or an email nobody has registered, is refused without saying which of the two was wrong.
- An account that an administrator has deactivated cannot be used to log in.

## Staying logged in

As a user, I don't want to log in every time I open the dashboard.

- An access token stays valid for about a week, then expires.
- An expired token is refused; the user has to log in again.

## My items

As a user, I keep a list of items, each with a title and an optional description.

- I can create an item; it belongs to me.
- I can see, change and delete my own items.
- I cannot see, change or delete items that belong to someone else.
- An administrator can see and manage every item.

## Item titles

- Every item must have a title.
- A title can't be too long; the dashboard allows titles of up to 255 characters.

## Browsing items

As a user with many items, I want to page through them.

- The item list shows the newest items first.
- I can ask for a page of items by saying how many to skip and how many to show.
- Each response also tells me how many items I have in total.
- A page shows a reasonable number of items by default.

</requirements>
